questions.title: Find the syntax errors
questions.text: The Python code contains **three** syntax errors. Rewrite it correctly.

scheme.mark_scheme: Closing bracket on line 1 (1); colon after the condition (1); print spelt correctly (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```python
mark = int(input("Mark: "))
if mark >= 50:
    print("Pass")
```

questions.title: Who finds syntax errors
questions.text: Explain how syntax errors are detected and reported.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The translator (compiler / interpreter) detects them during translation / syntax analysis (1)
- it reports an error message with the line number; the program does not run (1)
scheme.model_answer: The compiler or interpreter finds them when it translates the code and shows an error message with the line number; the program cannot run until they are fixed.

questions.title: Compiler or interpreter
questions.text: An interpreter usually stops at the first syntax error it reaches, while a compiler can list all the syntax errors in the program.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: Describe a logic error
questions.text: Describe a logic error and give an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The program runs but gives the wrong result because the algorithm is wrong (1)
- example: wrong operator / brackets in a calculation / wrong loop limit / wrong variable output (1)
scheme.model_answer: A logic error lets the program run but gives a wrong answer, e.g. average = a + b / 2 instead of (a + b) / 2.

questions.title: Brackets in a calculation
questions.text: The line should calculate the mean of three numbers. With a = 6, b = 9, c = 3 it outputs 16 instead of 6. Explain the error, name its type and write the correct line.

scheme.mark_scheme: Division is done before addition so only c is divided by 3 (1); logic error (1); average = (a + b + c) / 3 (1)
scheme.model_answer: Only c is divided by 3 because division happens before addition (6 + 9 + 1 = 16). This is a logic error. Correct: average = (a + b + c) / 3

questions.title: Trace to find the error
questions.text:
This code should output the largest number.

```python
numbers = [4, 9, 2]
largest = 0
for n in numbers:
    if n < largest:
        largest = n
print(largest)
```

Complete the trace table showing `largest` after each value of n.

scheme.mark_scheme: 4 → 0; 9 → 0; 2 → 0 (1 each). The comparison should be n > largest.

questions.title: Correct the condition
questions.text: Write the corrected condition for the code in the previous question.

scheme.mark_scheme: if n > largest: (1)
scheme.model_answer: if n > largest:

questions.title: Off-by-one
questions.text: The loop `for i in range(1, 10): print(i)` should print the numbers 1 to 10. What is wrong?

options.content: A syntax error: range needs three arguments
A logic error: it stops at 9, the limit should be 11
A runtime error: i goes out of range

scheme.mark_scheme: B

scheme.mark_scheme: Line 8 (1); PRINT "Well done, you took ", count, " attempts" (1)
scheme.model_answer: Line 8 — count is inside the quotes. Correct: PRINT "Well done, you took ", count, " attempts"

questions.title: Runtime error
questions.text: Describe a runtime error and give an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Occurs while the program is running and makes it crash / stop, although the syntax is correct (1)
- example: division by zero / index out of range / type mismatch / file not found (1)
scheme.model_answer: An error that happens while the program is running and makes it crash, e.g. dividing by zero.

questions.title: Handle the error
questions.text: Write Python code that asks for the number of pupils and outputs 100 divided by that number, **without crashing** if the user enters text or 0.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- input converted to int inside try (1)
- division and output inside try (1)

questions.title: Prevent an index error
questions.text: The array `Marks[1:30]` holds 30 marks. Write pseudocode that inputs a position and outputs the mark at that position, or an error message if the position is not valid.

scheme.mark_scheme: INPUT Position (1); IF Position >= 1 AND Position <= 30 THEN OUTPUT Marks[Position] (1); ELSE error message (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```pseudocode
INPUT Position
IF Position >= 1 AND Position <= 30 THEN
    OUTPUT Marks[Position]
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Position must be 1 to 30"
ENDIF
```

questions.title: Hardest to find
questions.text: Explain why logic errors are usually harder to find than syntax errors.

scheme.mark_scheme: No error message — the translator cannot detect them because the syntax is correct (1); the program runs normally, so wrong results are only found by testing / comparing with expected results (1)
scheme.model_answer: The code is grammatically correct, so the translator gives no error message; the program runs and only careful testing against expected results shows that the answer is wrong.

questions.title: Error types
questions.text: Programs can contain syntax, logic and runtime errors.

parts.title: Determine
parts.text: Determine the type of programming error by its description.

fields.label: (i) The programmer misspelt a statement while coding.
(ii) The program tries to access an element outside the bounds of the array.
(iii) Brackets are used incorrectly in a calculation.

scheme.mark_scheme: (i) syntax error (1); (ii) runtime / execution error (1); (iii) logic error (1)
scheme.model_answer:
(i) Syntax error
(ii) Runtime error
(iii) Logic error

parts.title: Detection
parts.text: Complete the table to show how each type of error is detected.

scheme.mark_scheme: Syntax: translator / compiler / interpreter error message (1); Logic: testing and comparing actual with expected results / trace table / dry run (1); Runtime: program crashes / stops with an error message while running (1)
scheme.model_answer:
| Type | Detected by |
|---|---|
| Syntax | The translator reports it with the line number |
| Logic | Testing with expected results / trace tables |
| Runtime | The program crashes while running |

parts.title: Translator
parts.text: Describe **one** mistake that the translator would catch and explain why the translator cannot catch logic errors.

scheme.mark_scheme: Mistake: syntax error e.g. missing bracket / colon / misspelt keyword (1); logic errors follow the syntax rules (1); the translator does not know what the program should do, so it cannot see the result is wrong (1)
scheme.model_answer: Forgetting to close a bracket would be caught. Logic errors are written in correct syntax, and the translator does not know what the program is supposed to do, so it cannot tell the answer is wrong.

questions.title: Finding logic errors
questions.text:
The program should output the total and the average of the marks entered. It stops when -1 is entered.

```python
1  total = 0
2  count = 0
3  mark = int(input("Mark: "))
4  while mark != -1:
5      total = total + mark
6      mark = int(input("Mark: "))
7  average = total / count
8  print("Total:", total, "Average:", average)
```

parts.title: Trace
parts.text: The user enters 7, 5, 9, -1. Complete the trace table with the value of mark, total and count after each pass of the loop.

scheme.mark_scheme: 7 → total 7; 5 → 12; 9 → 21; count stays 0 in every row (1 per row + 1 for count column)

parts.title: What happens
parts.text: Explain what happens when line 7 is executed and state the type of error.

scheme.mark_scheme: count is 0 so total / count divides by zero and the program crashes (1); runtime error (1)
scheme.model_answer: count is still 0, so 21 / 0 is a division by zero and the program crashes — a runtime error.

parts.title: Cause
parts.text: Identify the logic error that causes this problem and write the missing line.

scheme.mark_scheme: count is never increased inside the loop (1); add count = count + 1 inside the loop (after line 5) (1)
scheme.model_answer: count is never increased; add count = count + 1 inside the loop, after line 5.

parts.title: Protect
parts.text: Rewrite lines 7–8 so that the program does not crash if the first mark entered is -1.

scheme.mark_scheme: if count > 0 / count != 0 (1); calculate and print the average inside (1); else output a message such as "No marks entered" (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```python
if count > 0:
    average = total / count
    print("Total:", total, "Average:", average)
else:
    print("No marks entered")
```

scheme.mark_scheme: The program will likely encounter a type mismatch or runtime error (1)
scheme.model_answer: A type mismatch (runtime) error — the program crashes when it tries to use the text as a number.

parts.title: Translator mistake
parts.text: Describe a mistake a programmer might make while writing this code that the translator would catch.

scheme.mark_scheme: Syntax error, e.g. forgetting to close a parenthesis / brace / missing colon (1)
scheme.model_answer: A syntax error such as forgetting the colon at the end of an if statement.

parts.title: Handle
parts.text: Write code that inputs def and keeps asking until a whole number is entered, without crashing.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- loop until valid (1)
- input converted to int inside try (1)
- except ValueError catches text (1)
- error message shown and asked again / loop exits when valid (1)

parts.title: Index
parts.text: The players' names are stored in `players = ["Ali", "Bob", ... ]` with 11 elements. Explain what happens when the code runs `print(players[11])`.

scheme.mark_scheme: Indexes run from 0 to 10, so index 11 is outside the bounds (1); runtime error — index out of range / program crashes (1)
scheme.model_answer: The indexes go from 0 to 10, so index 11 is outside the array; the program stops with an index-out-of-range runtime error.

parts.title: Debugging
parts.text: Describe **two** techniques the programmer could use to locate errors in the program.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): trace table / dry run; breakpoints; stepping line by line; watch variables; print statements; testing with planned data; reading error messages
scheme.model_answer: 1 A trace table records each variable's value while dry-running the code. 2 Breakpoints and stepping run the code line by line to see where values go wrong.

summary: The three types of programming error — syntax, logic and runtime (execution) errors — what causes each, many examples in Python and pseudocode, when and how each is detected (translator messages, testing, trace tables, crashes), how to prevent runtime errors with validation and exception handling, debugging techniques, and identifying errors from descriptions in exam questions.

blocks.content: A **bug** is an **error in a program** that stops it working as intended. **Debugging** is the process of **finding, identifying and correcting** errors.

blocks.title: The three types of error at a glance
rows: The code **breaks the grammar rules** of the language
An operation **cannot be carried out** while the program runs
The **translator** (compiler / interpreter) with an error message and line number
**Testing** (compare actual with expected results), **trace tables**, **dry runs**
The program **stops** with an error message (exception)
`area = 2 * r * r` instead of `3.14 * r * r`
Division by zero, index out of range

blocks.content:
- "The programmer **misspelt a statement** while coding" → **syntax error**.
- "**Incorrectly using brackets** in calculations" → **logic error**.
- "A program tries to access an **element outside the bounds of the array**" → **runtime (execution) error**.
- "Text is entered where a **number** is expected" → **runtime** error (type mismatch).
- "The program outputs the **wrong variable**" → **logic error**.
A mistake that **breaks the grammar (syntax) rules of the programming language**, so the translator cannot understand the code. The program **will not compile or run** until it is corrected.

if mark > 50            # SyntaxError: expected ':'
    print("Pass"        # SyntaxError: '(' was never closed
blocks.caption: Syntax errors and the translator's messages

items.title: How syntax errors are detected
items.content:
- The **translator** checks the code during **syntax analysis** and reports each error with a **line number** and a **message**.
- A **compiler** usually lists **all** the syntax errors it finds and produces **no** executable file.
- An **interpreter** stops at the **first** error it reaches.
- Many editors (IDEs) **underline** syntax errors while you type.

items.title: How to fix them
items.content:
- Read the **error message** and look at the line given — and the line **before** it (a missing bracket is often reported one line later).
- Correct one error at a time and re-run.

blocks.content: A mistake in the **algorithm**: the program **runs without crashing but gives the wrong result** or behaves incorrectly. The syntax is correct, so the **translator cannot detect** it.

blocks.title: Common causes of logic errors
rows: printing the total **before** the loop has added the values
`total` not set to 0 before a loop

blocks.content:
numbers = [4, 9, 2]
largest = 0
for n in numbers:
    if n < largest:          # logic error: should be n > largest
        largest = n
print(largest)               # prints 0 — expected 9
blocks.caption: A logic error found with a trace table

blocks.title: Trace table that reveals the logic error
blocks.content:
| n | n < largest? | largest |
|---|---|---|
| — | — | 0 |
| 4 | False | 0 |
| 9 | False | 0 |
| 2 | False | 0 |

The output **0** is not the expected **9**, and the trace shows `largest` never changes → the comparison must be `n > largest`.

items.title: How logic errors are detected
items.content:
- **Testing** with normal, boundary and erroneous data and **comparing the actual result with the expected result**.
- **Dry runs** and **trace tables** — following the code by hand to see where the values go wrong.
- **Debugger** tools: breakpoints, stepping through the code line by line, watching variables.
- Adding temporary **print statements** to show the values of variables.

items.title: Why they are the hardest to find
items.content:
- There is **no error message** — the program looks as if it works.
- The wrong result may only appear for **some** data (e.g. only at a boundary).

blocks.content: An error that occurs **while the program is running**: an instruction **cannot be carried out**, so the program **crashes** or stops unexpectedly, even though the syntax is correct. It often depends on the **data** being processed.

blocks.title: Common runtime errors
rows: **Index out of range** — accessing an element outside the bounds of an array
**Undefined variable** used before it has a value
the loop condition never becomes false

blocks.content:
marks = [7, 9, 4]
print(marks[3])            # IndexError: list index out of range

n = int(input("How many students? "))   # user types "ten" → ValueError
print(100 / n)                           # user types 0     → ZeroDivisionError
blocks.caption: Runtime errors

items.title: Preventing runtime errors — validation
items.content:
- Check input **before** using it: `if n != 0:` before dividing; check an index is between **0** and **length − 1**; check the input is a **number**.
- Check that a **file exists** before opening it.

items.title: Handling runtime errors — exception handling
items.content:
- Put risky code in a `try` block; if an error happens, the `except` block runs **instead of crashing**, showing a helpful message.
- Other languages: `try … catch` (Java, JavaScript, C++), `On Error` (VB).

blocks.caption: Handling runtime errors with try … except

blocks.content:
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:30] OF INTEGER
INPUT Position
IF Position >= 1 AND Position <= 30 THEN
    OUTPUT Marks[Position]
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Position must be 1 to 30"
ENDIF
blocks.caption: Preventing an index error in pseudocode

blocks.title: Debugging techniques
rows: Shows the **type** of error and the **line** — for syntax and runtime errors
Follows the values of variables step by step — finds **logic** errors
Stop the program at a chosen line to look at the variables
Execute **one line at a time** and watch the values change
Shows chosen variables continuously while stepping
Output intermediate values to see where they become wrong
Normal, boundary and erroneous data find logic and runtime errors

blocks.title: Identify and correct — exam style
blocks.content:
```pseudocode
1  compnum ← 50
2  count ← 1
3  INPUT guess
4  WHILE guess <> compnum DO
5      count ← count + 1
6      INPUT guess
7  ENDWHILE
8  PRINT "Well done, you took count attempts"
```
**Line 8** contains a **logic error**: the word `count` is inside the quotes, so the text "count" is printed instead of the **value** of the variable. Correct form: `PRINT "Well done, you took ", count, " attempts"`.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Determine the type of programming error. (i) The programmer misspelt a statement while coding. (ii) Incorrectly using brackets in calculations. (iii) Accessing an element outside the bounds of an array. [3]**
(i) **Syntax** error (1); (ii) **logic** error (1); (iii) **runtime (execution)** error (1).

**Q: Describe a logic error. [2]**
The program **runs** but produces the **wrong result** (1) because the **algorithm** is wrong, e.g. a wrong operator or formula (1).

**Q: Describe an error that will occur if text is entered into a variable that should hold a number. [1]**
A **type mismatch / runtime error** — the program crashes when it tries to use the text as a number (1).

**Q: Explain why a translator cannot detect logic errors. [2]**
The code **follows the syntax rules** of the language (1); the translator does not know **what the program is meant to do**, so it cannot tell the result is wrong (1).

- Calling an index-out-of-range error a **logic** error — it is a **runtime** error (the program crashes).
- Saying a logic error "stops the program" — it **runs** and gives a **wrong** answer.
- Writing "logic" alone when the mark scheme asks for "**logical error**" / "logic error" — use the full term.
- Thinking the translator finds all errors — it finds only **syntax** errors.
